item.title: When “Helpful” Relatives Are Actually Hypercritical
item.description:
Family Dynamics

When “Helpful” Relatives Are Actually Hypercritical

How constant criticism masquerades as concern, and what to do about it.

Posted July 28, 2026

Key points
  • Hypercritical relatives often disguise hurtful comments as concern, honesty, or help.
  • Respecting a family member does not require accepting disrespect.
  • Allies can interrupt harmful criticism and protect relatives with less power.

In many families, even those considered good, constant criticism is often normalized.

“You’re getting fat.”

“Why can’t you be more like your sister?”

“That haircut isn’t flattering.”

“You’re too sensitive.”

The criticism is framed as concern, and the theme is always the same: You are never quite good enough.

What Is Hypercriticism?

Hypercriticism is a pattern of frequent, personal shaming or perfectionistic judgments of others. It differs from constructive feedback, which is specific, proportionate, supportive, and, ideally, invited.

In families, chronic criticism may be framed as “helping,” “making you tougher,” or “pushing you to do better.” But it rarely achieves those goals. Demeaning words are far more likely to hurt than help. For instance, studies of “fat talk” in mother-child relationships found that daughters were more likely to internalize these critical messages, contributing to body shame, negative body image, anxiety, and depression.1, 2

Who Tends to Be Hypercritical?

Hypercriticism about appearance and other personal characteristics may be especially common among female relatives and directed toward other women in the family. Male relatives may also initiate, reinforce, or participate in this criticism.

Generational differences can add another layer. When criticism comes from a parent, grandparent, or older relative, family hierarchies and expectations about respecting elders may make the recipient feel unable to respond or defend herself.

Hypercritical individuals often reserve their harshest commentary for close relatives. They may never speak to a friend or coworker in the same demeaning way because they understand that such behavior carries consequences in other relationships. Within families, however, closeness, obligation, and demands for respect can be used as permission to say things that would be unacceptable elsewhere.

What Drives Hypercriticism?

Hypercriticism may be rooted in jealousy, envy, shame, or insecurity. For example, someone who struggles with their own weight may focus on a relative’s slight weight gain, while someone dissatisfied with their relationship status may criticize another person for being single. Such comments may reflect deflection or projection, allowing the critic to redirect attention away from their own feelings of inadequacy or low self-worth.

To Respond or Not to Respond

People learn how to treat you partly through what you accept and what you challenge. In families, however, status, generational hierarchies, and power differences can make speaking up complicated. Even a calm response may be labeled “disrespectful”—but respecting a relative does not require accepting disrespect.

If directly confronting the person feels unsafe or socially costly, quiet resistance is also an option. A calm, neutral expression can communicate that the unsolicited criticism is neither welcome nor amusing.

A Call to Action

Allies are essential in challenging hypercriticism within families. This may be the outspoken cousin who is willing to risk backlash, the grandfather who notices your hurt, or a relative closer in age or status to the critic. These family members can use their influence to interrupt harmful comments and protect those with less power.

Words matter. Family should be a soft place to land after facing a world that can already be harsh. Families can grow, change, and do better, but change requires intention. Awareness is the first step. Practice is the second.

Before offering criticism, THINK: Is it True, Helpful, Inspiring, Necessary, and Kind?

item.title: The Irish Giant Betrayed: The Ethics of the Public Gaze
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

The Irish Giant Betrayed: The Ethics of the Public Gaze

The legacy of displaying lives and bodies, and the threat of the fixed gaze.

Posted July 28, 2026

Key points
  • Sideshow exhibits that featured human oddities once amused millions.
  • Freak shows’ appeal faded, but popular attractions still spark morbid curiosity.
  • The fixed gaze objectifies, blurring lines between curiosity and cruelty.

Early memories encoded visually prove remarkably sticky. A recollection that is hardest for me to forget is a childhood trip to a carnival freak show.

Our small family had traveled to a fair for the tame thrill rides. If I rode a carousel, the experience is now lost or overshadowed.

The attraction there that persists tenaciously in memory, the one that I must have insisted on seeing, was advertised as the two-headed baby. We’d been ballyhooed into a striped tent. I must have tugged my father in. The come-on pushed the buttons for exoticism—the promise of physical oddity and foreignness. (This was the first time I heard the word “Siamese,” for example, a vivid instance of the way visual and auditory recall conspires.)

But once the drapery parted, the infant conjoined twins proved a great anticlimax, consisting of only an Asian-stylized concrete sculpture sunk into an aquarium. Because the exhibit was placed at the exit with no re-entry possible, this joke was on the visitor. An old-fashioned “humbug,” it moved the crowd along, profitably. This way to the egress.

Two other human exhibits pushed the buttons of otherness (“othering” in modern psychological parlance) more bluntly. The first was a purported Hawaiian princess, dressed in a flowered muumuu, who towered over her diminutive dashiki-clad consort. A comic narrator on stage provided a spiel that my 6-year-old brain couldn’t process. On the next stage, a geek invited the audience to poke hatpins through his biceps, and then more strangely, patiently guided more piercing through his cheek, the needle passing through his tongue, and then out the other cheek.

"Little Egypt" performed daring dances at U.S. expositions around the turn of the 19th century.
Source: Benjamin Falk/Public Domain

When my mother caught up with us outside and discovered where we’d been, my father was in for it.

Titillation vs. Uplift

Freak shows, an invention in Europe of some antiquity, became popular in North America in the late 19th century. Yielding to growing medical understanding, ethical qualms, and better manners, the kind of attraction that I witnessed had nearly vanished here by the mid-20th century.

In their heyday, though, as regular features at amusement parks and circuses, exhibits of human oddity commanded the attention of the democracy, out-attracting sober and uplifting experiences like a visit to the art museum or a night at the symphony.

The spread of the eight-hour day and the half-day Saturday, victories for exploited, overworked labor, left millions with free time that they filled not with Victorian refinement and edification that elite and paternalistic elements had hoped for, but sometimes with thrill and unchecked prurience of amusement rides and the cabinets of curiosities called dime museums.

Crowded seaside boardwalks hosted semipermanent sideshows that featured performers who tolerated and capitalized on prying eyes. Hoochie-coochie dancers attracted the male gaze. Tattooed ladies (shockingly so then) inked and exhibited their bodies transgressively. Some others exploited natural but unusual physical differences.

The Long and Short of It

One such, General Tom Thumb, born Charles Sherwood Stratton in 1838, became the most famous human attraction at P.T. Barnum’s travelling circus. Stratton, whose growth had halted at a reported 25 inches, the result of a pituitary malady, turned disability into fame and fortune.

A talented singer, dancer, and comic impressionist, he entertained large audiences in North America, the British Isles, and India. He met Abraham Lincoln and was presented to Queen Victoria. A wealthy man, Stratton bailed his impulsive friend Barnum out of financial ruin and became the impresario’s business partner.

Stratton’s wife, Lavinia, also of short stature, performed at his side before curious audiences. In day-to-day life, glances remain brief. Thus, most who bear the weight of fixed, unapologetic scrutiny will regard the experience as unpleasant or provocative. (Evolution has prepared us to detect the threat of the predatory gaze.) Steeled to prying eyes, however, Lavinia conceded that their lives “belonged to the public.” Her story seems to be one more of agency than exploitation. When people stared, she, secure in her boundaries, stared right back.

These two American success stories of resilience and seized opportunity are the reassuring kind that audiences liked to hear.

The Irish Giant in Life and Death

A century before, however, the life experience of Charles Byrne, who was briefly on public display in London as “The Irish Giant,” stood in desolate contrast. Against his dying wishes that he should be buried anonymously out of the reach of curiosity, his remains became a museum exhibit for two-and-a-quarter centuries.

Born in Belfast, Byrne grew to seven feet seven inches in an era when men averaged about five feet five inches. Byrne would stand well above a current NBA forward today. Social science research has confirmed that normally commanding height confers a social advantage, as those of shorter stature generally will defer and give way, as in a cramped subway car, for example. To be put on display, though, reverses this power dynamic. Similarly, zoo visitors may find captive lions and tigers humorous rather than frightening.

Fascinated by the ethical and moral issues that Byrne’s brief celebrity and his heartbreakingly unfulfilled last wishes raise, the cultural and social historian David A. Gerber studied Byrne’s notoriety. Gerber noted that this was far from a story about victory over disability, or about adaptability and pluck; acromegaly had so narrowed Byrne’s options that his parents sold him for display, to be exploited and objectified as an object of public curiosity.

The Irish Giant Betrayed

We know little else of the Irish Giant’s life other than the betrayal of his desperate last wishes.

Living in shabby London rooms, salient of his impending death, his pain poorly controlled by heavy drinking, Byrne begged his friends to seal his corpse in a lead coffin and sink it below the waves where it would lie forever unregarded.

That his body might instead be stolen by grave robbers and exhibited, a reasonable fear given the moneymaking potential of his extraordinary skeleton within, became the waking nightmare in his final days.

Byrne’s body was indeed diverted into the possession of an undertaker who had been bribed to boil away the flesh. The bones were then delivered to a famous anatomist who operated his own cabinet of curiosities on the side. For two and a half centuries after, the skeleton of the Irish Giant remained, amidst controversy and, again, against his wishes, on exhibit.

Have We Outgrown the Freak Show?

While the tawdry carnival freak show of my sharp, early memory has yielded to common decency, a similar attraction, staged with vastly more sophistication, has appealed to macabre fascination.

The traveling exhibit Body Worlds, which rests on fragile justifications of science and art, presents flayed, polymerized human corpses posed whimsically—ice skaters mid-pas de deux, dead basketball players driving toward the hoop, a skinned “yoga lady”—has to date attracted an estimated 58 million gawkers spared from bearing the weight of a returned stare.

item.title: Hidden Secrets of Psychotherapy: What Is "Clinical Wisdom"?
item.description:
Therapy

Hidden Secrets of Psychotherapy: What Is "Clinical Wisdom"?

Where clinical wisdom comes from, and how it's made use of in therapy.

Posted July 28, 2026

Key points
  • Clinical wisdom is a collective, evolving knowledge base from over a century of psychotherapy.
  • Clinical wisdom blends psychological, philosophical, and spiritual perspectives on the human condition.
  • Psychotherapy’s limitations must be accepted to avoid frustration or disappointment in therapy.

This is Part 2 of a series.

In Part 1 of this series, I introduced the concept of what I call "clinical wisdom" in the practice of psychotherapy. What is it, where does it come from, and how can we make constructive use of it in clinical practice?

Freud's psychoanalytic couch.
Source: JRennocks/Wikimedia Commons/CC BY 4.0

What Is "Clinical Wisdom"?

I define clinical wisdom as an eclectic, collective compendium of archetypal and pragmatic psychological, philosophical, existential, and spiritual knowledge derived and distilled from more than a century of psychotherapeutic practice or research, as well as from other more venerable religious, spiritual, or healing traditions.

Psychotherapy has evolved dramatically since its beginnings, first described by Freud as "psychoanalysis" (see Breuer and Freud, 1895), and was further developed by Adler, Rank, Jung, Frankl, Rogers, May, Perls, Ellis, Beck, Linehan, and many others. Indeed, much has been discovered over the past hundred years about the enigmatic and mysterious human mind, psyche, or soul: what truly motivates, drives, influences, sustains, and inspires us, what causes us to become depressed, anxious, sad, or angry, and what helps to keep us sane, happy, healthy, stable, balanced, and whole.

Contemporary psychotherapists (e.g., psychologists, psychiatrists, and other mental health professionals) have, thanks in part especially to the contributions of existential therapy (see May et al., 1958; Frankl, 1969; and Yalom, 1980), also gained a clearer comprehension of the universal human condition: the inescapable existential “givens” or immutable facts of life, like aloneness, freedom, responsibility, and finitude; our “ultimate concerns”; our incessant striving for survival, love, relatedness, significance, meaning, purpose, recognition, and immortality; the inevitability of loss, suffering, sickness, and ultimately, death; the perennial problem of evil; and the apparently inherent human need for some sort of philosophical, religious, or spiritual perspective or foundation upon which to resiliently stand in life.

In the field of psychopathology, for instance, the American Psychiatric Association's DSM-5-TR (2022), despite its serious drawbacks, is a veritable cornucopia of valuable and practical information regarding the symptomatology, typical course, epidemiology, demographics, diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment of mental disorders. This and various other kinds and sources of clinical wisdom have traditionally been handed down from master psychotherapist to apprentice or disciple, from supervisor to supervisee, from training analyst to trainee, from professor to pupil, from author or researcher to student, growing ever more refined, developing, maturing, and constantly evolving over time. Drawing upon the seminal ideas and insights of eminent pioneering psychotherapists, clinical wisdom refers to what has been cumulatively learned and discovered over the past century of clinical practice about the human condition, the existential facts of life, and the hard-won wisdom psychotherapists have found crucial in helping people to live life more meaningfully, passionately, productively, and creatively. Not by denying, minimizing, or avoiding the darkest, most dreadful existential realities of life—like suffering, isolation, meaninglessness, mortality, and the disturbing fact of evil in the world—but rather by encouraging patients to consciously confront them.

The Clinical Wisdom of Managing Unrealistic Expectations

What, then, are some of the key components of what I am calling "clinical wisdom"? What are these esoteric, hidden, quintessential secrets of psychotherapy? Let us begin from the beginning. The psychotherapy project and process start with the way both the prospective psychotherapist and patient see themselves and their respective roles. The psychotherapist, who has already been exposed to some of this clinical wisdom by dint of their professional training and experience, sees themself as a helper, guide, or expert, someone who strives to alleviate and minister to the suffering, confusion, despair, and existential crises of others. This is their raison d'être, their reason for being. The patient (which some clinicians call the client) perceives themself as the recipient of such expert assistance, guidance, and support, toward the goal of alleviating or at least mitigating or suppressing their symptoms, suffering, and struggles with themself, others, and existence itself. At some level, the patient or client believes they can be helped, and the psychotherapist believes they can be helpful. But, at a deeper level, both the patient (and practitioner) may be seeking something that psychotherapy cannot actually provide, such as a "cure," complete freedom from complexes and symptoms, immunity to existential loss, suffering, aloneness, and evil, perfect relationships, or persisting so-called "happiness." (See my prior post.)

Herein lies a fundamental element of clinical wisdom: Psychotherapy, like everything else in life, has limitations. This is an essential fact for patients and clinicians to comprehend and accept so that neither approaches therapy with unrealistic expectations as to what it can provide. For the patient, such awareness and acceptance can prevent profound frustration, disappointment, and premature termination of treatment. For the psychotherapist, such basic clinical wisdom can make treatment goals more realistic and attainable and the phenomenon of so-called clinician "burnout" less likely.
